chapter_theme: The invocation (காப்பு) of Thiruvalluvar Njanam, a late Siddhar work attributed to Thiruvalluvar and not by the author of the Kural: eight lines of போற்றி to Brahma and Vishnu filling cosmos and body, the fullness, the sun-and-moon light, Agastya of sweet Tamil, the poet's guru, the lotus of the sushumna in the left channel and Guha seated in the kundalini. It places the work in the Agastya lineage of the medical and yogic Siddhars, not in the Kural's world.

1622.reading: Praise to Brahma and Vishnu who fill cosmos and body; praise to the grace of the undivided fullness; praise to the light of sun and moon girt by the mandala; praise to Agastya who speaks sweet Tamil; praise to my guru whom the eight directions praise; praise to the lotus of the sushumna in the left channel; praise to Guha seated within the kundalini; praise forever to the feet of the guru-sage.
1622.nuance: The invocation is wholly a Siddhar's: அண்டம்பிண்டம், பரிபூரணம், சுழுமுனை, குண்டலி, and Agastya and the guru rather than Siva by name. The attribution to Valluvar rests on the title alone; the Kural's own invocation names only the Primal Lord. இடைகலையின் சுழுமுனையின் கமலம், the sushumna's lotus in the left channel, is odd as anatomy and may mean the lotus reached through the left (moon) breath.

links.note: Two Siddhar invocations that place the guru in the body: Romarishi's protection is the guru's foot that is the root circle; here the guru is praised beside the lotus of the sushumna and Guha within the kundalini.

The Kural's invocation names one Primal Lord as the first of the world; the work that borrows Valluvar's name invokes Brahma, Vishnu, the sun-moon light, Agastya, the guru and Guha in the body's channels, which is one reason the attribution is not taken seriously.
